catalog_locator: 'The Accent', p.7; immediate future tense, p.49
catalog_quote: THE ACCENT. The accent is invariably on the last syllable but one. When two vowels come together they are usually pronounced as close vowels, in which case the accent is thrown back to the first of these vowels, as ku-leiUiy [scanned-garbled example] to dun. When a suffix is used the accent is moved so as to be on the last syllable but one. There are but few monosyllabic words in the Sagalla dialect. ... [p.49] The immediate future is formed by the use of the same pronominal prefixes as in the mediate future, but without the syllable ./e- [scanned for je-], and slightly throwing the accent on the final syllable of the verb, as — ni-lima, I will cultivate. The final -a of this tense is often changed into -a^ga [scanned for -a'ga], as — ni-lim-a'gay [scanned for ni-lim-a'ga,] I will cultivate.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract only says that the East African Bantu sample spans fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to demarcative-penultimate-stress languages (Swahili) and that penultimate accent drove the diachrony; it does not name Sagalla/Saghala or say where its stress falls. The thesis body, where Saghala would be treated, could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Catalog item is Sagalla = Saghala/Kisagalla (Guthrie E74b), sister of Davida/Dawida (E74a) within Taita (Odden 2006 p.33 wording: 'Mbololo is one of the dialects of Davida (E74a), a sister language of Saghala (E74b)'). Patin's work (2002 MA thesis, 2009 Faits de Langues) on the Teri dialect of Saghala remains unopened (paywalled/unheld per prior notes).

new_statements.translation: [p.483] (c) languages with a culmination of length, but not of pitch, on the penultimate (languages with distinctive prosodemes [i.e. tone], but without a length opposition): Nande and Konzo; Langi; Nyanja and Chewa; Makonde; Shambaa, Bondei, Zigula, Ngulu; Mwani, Comorian, Pokomo, Mijikenda; Asu; Davida and Saghala; Chaga; [...] [p.449] 2.7.3. The tonal system of Saghala is not yet well known, but it seems to have much in common with that of Mijikenda. In fact, the classification of Saghala in the same group as Davida shows the limits of the lexicostatistic method.

new_statements.relation_note: Placement agrees with the catalog (Wray 1894: 'accent invariably on the last syllable but one' -> penult). Philippson adds the type: Saghala is a tone language ('prosodèmes distinctifs', tone system like Mijikenda's) whose penultimate prominence is durational (length culmination, no pitch culmination), i.e. a demarcative penult accent coexisting with lexical/grammatical tone. This also upgrades the existing statement held by the project for this same work, which rested on the theses.fr abstract only and did not name Saghala: the full text names 'da∫ida et saghala' explicitly at p.483 and lists Saghala among the languages recorded first-hand (p.515).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Saghala (E74b) is classed, from the author's own field notes, as a language with distinctive tones (prosodèmes distinctifs) and no vowel-length contrast, in which word prominence falls on the penultimate syllable and is realised as lengthening of the penult (culmination de longueur), not as a pitch peak; its tone system is said to be poorly known and to resemble Mijikenda's rather than Davida's.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Saghala; the author flags Saghala as poorly documented (no cross in Tableau 1, p.72; 'pas encore bien connu', p.449) and gives no Saghala-specific synopsis in the Annexe (only Davida, p.512).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson treats 'saghala (E 74b)' of his groupe XX (Taita) from his own field notes (p.515), alongside da∫ida (E 74a); no sub-dialect of Saghala is named (Patin's later work is on the Teri dialect). The catalog record is Wray's 'Sagalla dialect' of Taita; same language.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held Wray 1894 djvu text at printed p.7 and p.49; the p.7 page scan downloaded now confirms the wording and fixes the garbled example ('ku-leila, to dun'). (2) The classification rests on an 1894 SPCK missionary primer (pedagogical grammar/sketch) with an impressionistic, tone-blind 'accent' statement. For Sagalla proper Glottolog lists nothing better (2 refs: Wray 1894; unpublished Verbi & Austin notes), and repository searches (UoN, KU) found no Sagalla phonology thesis (the held UoN 2016 MA is a loanword study; its bibliography cites Mwasusu 2012 on Kidawida stress, a different language). However Breteler 2018's bibliography and Crossref show modern tone-focused fieldwork on Saghala by Patin (2002 MA thesis on the 'systeme accentuel'; 2009 Faits de Langues article), neither held nor open; held Breteler 2018 relays Patin's data
